content.problem: Can a small model tell horizontal bars from vertical bars in noisy images? We’ll create the images locally and train a convolutional classifier on CPU. You’ll then test images from a different random seed and read a confusion matrix. The task is small enough to inspect without downloading a dataset.
content.idea: A convolution combines a local input patch with weights reused across spatial positions. Layout, stride and padding decide which pixels contribute to each output. Trace one position first; the full feature map repeats that same rule.
objectives: Generate images with an explicit label rule
Pool spatial responses and retain class scores
Read a confusion matrix rather than a success label

sections.title: Trace one convolution output
sections.body:
For one output cell, take the matching \(3\times3\) image patch, multiply element by element by one filter, sum over the patch's height, width, and input channels, then add that filter's bias. The same filter values are reused at the next location; only the selected pixels move. The independent NumPy dot product checks one interior cell before training.

The 5-by-5 diagram is a separate shape example: with stride one and no padding, the top-left patch can move to three positions across and three down, giving a 3-by-3 output map. The trained images are 8-by-8, so the same kernel yields 6-by-6 positions. Use the confusion matrix afterward to see which held-out orientations were mistaken.

check.prompt: What stays shared when the kernel moves?
check.answer: The filter weights and bias. The input patch changes. This is different from learning unrelated weights at every spatial location.

sections.title: Generate images with an explicit label rule
sections.body:
Each example is an \(8\times8\times1\) image. Horizontal bars are class zero and vertical bars are class one; the bar's interior position varies, and Gaussian noise perturbs every pixel. Alternating labels keeps the generated split balanced. A different seed creates new held-out images without changing the label rule.

In the retained held-out image, a bright horizontal band appears around row 3, while other pixels remain near zero with noise. Inspecting an image and its label makes the task concrete before the CNN is fit. This generator has no perspective, occlusion, or natural objects, so its result says nothing about photographs.

sections.title: Derive the convolution output shape
sections.body:
The input layout is \((B,H,W,C)\). With an \(8\times8\) image and a \(3\times3\) filter, VALID padding and stride one allow \(8-3+1=6\) positions along each spatial axis. Four output channels mean four learned filters, so each image produces a \(6\times6\times4\) activation array. The kernel shape is \((3,3,1,4)\) with four bias values.

The patch reference uses cross-correlation, the operation used by this convolution API: it does not flip the filter. Matching the NumPy result at the selected output checks channel order, patch indexing, and bias addition before the optimizer can obscure a layout error.

sections.title: Pool spatial responses and retain class scores
sections.body:
After ReLU, averaging spatial axes \(1\) and \(2\) turns each \(6\times6\) map into one value per filter. The result retains four features per image, regardless of where the bar appears. That invariance fits orientation classification, but it discards location information that a localization task would need.

The head produces two raw class scores. Pass those logits and integer labels directly to the stable cross-entropy; applying softmax first is unnecessary and changes the expected input. The NumPy reference subtracts the largest score before log-sum-exp and averages over images.

sections.title: Read a confusion matrix rather than a success label
sections.body:
Rows in the matrix are true classes and columns are predicted classes. The retained counts are \([[12,0],[0,12]]\): all 12 horizontal and all 12 vertical held-out images land on the diagonal. The matrix totals 24, and its trace divided by 24 equals the reported accuracy \(1.0\); held-out mean loss is \(0.015700625\).

A horizontal-only baseline would get 12 of 24 correct, or \(0.5\), because the set is balanced. If an off-diagonal count appears after a change, its row tells you the true orientation and its column the predicted one; inspect examples from that cell. Zero observed errors is not a guarantee on other images.

buildSteps.title: 1. Generate two disjoint synthetic splits
buildSteps.instruction: Create main.py. Print a training image as an \(8\times8\) array if you want to inspect the task before fitting.
buildSteps.code:
# Step 1 — 1. Generate two disjoint synthetic splits: Two seeds produce separate examples.
from flax import nnx
import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp
import numpy as np
import optax
def bars(seed,n,noise=.08):
    rng=np.random.default_rng(seed)
    images=np.zeros((n,8,8,1),np.float32)
    labels=np.arange(n,dtype=np.int32)%2
    for i,label in enumerate(labels):
        position=int(rng.integers(2,6))
        if label==0:images[i,position,:,0]=1.
        else:images[i,:,position,0]=1.
    # Accumulate the next contribution into `images`.
    images+=rng.normal(0,noise,images.shape).astype(np.float32)
    return jnp.array(images),jnp.array(labels)
train_x,train_y=bars(20,48)
test_x,test_y=bars(21,24)
# Check tensor shape invariant: `train_x.shape==(48,8,8,1) and test_x.shape==(24,8,8,1)`
assert train_x.shape==(48,8,8,1) and test_x.shape==(24,8,8,1)
assert not np.array_equal(np.asarray(train_x[:24]),np.asarray(test_x))
buildSteps.explanation: Two seeds produce separate examples. Both labels are balanced by construction; noise can make orientation harder as its scale grows.

buildSteps.title: 2. Build and independently inspect the convolution
buildSteps.instruction: Append the small CNN and the patch dot-product check before defining an optimizer.
buildSteps.code:
# Step 2 — 2. Build and independently inspect the convolution
# Define `BarCNN` module / container with explicit state and forward pass:
class BarCNN(nnx.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        rngs=nnx.Rngs(0)
        self.conv=nnx.Conv(1,4,(3,3),padding='VALID',rngs=rngs)
        self.head=nnx.Linear(4,2,rngs=rngs)
    def __call__(self,x):
        features=jnp.mean(nnx.relu(self.conv(x)),axis=(1,2))
        return self.head(features)
model=BarCNN()
raw=model.conv(train_x[:1])
# Check tensor shape invariant: `raw.shape==(1,6,6,4)`
assert raw.shape==(1,6,6,4)
# Transfer the device result to the host for an independent NumPy comparison.
patch=np.asarray(train_x[0,:3,:3,:])
# Transfer the device result to the host for an independent NumPy comparison.
kernel=np.asarray(model.conv.kernel[...])
expected=np.sum(patch*kernel[:,:,:,0])+np.asarray(model.conv.bias[...])[0]
np.testing.assert_allclose(raw[0,0,0,0],expected,rtol=1e-5,atol=1e-6)
def loss(m,x,y):return jnp.mean(optax.softmax_cross_entropy_with_integer_labels(m(x),y))
optimizer=nnx.Optimizer(model,optax.adam(.03),wrt=nnx.Param)
@nnx.jit
def train_step(m,o,x,y):
    value,grads=nnx.value_and_grad(loss)(m,x,y)
    # Apply the parameter gradients to the mutable Flax model and optimizer state.
    o.update(m,grads)
    return value
buildSteps.explanation: The first output at \((0,0)\) consumes exactly the top-left \(3\times3\) patch. The NumPy result validates filter orientation and layout.

buildSteps.title: 3. Fit, then measure the held-out split once
buildSteps.instruction: Append \(80\) full-batch updates, stable NumPy loss, and confusion accounting. Every update uses only train_x/train_y.
buildSteps.code:
# Step 3 — 3. Fit, then measure the held-out split once: The output is a measured CPU result for synthetic bars.
initial=float(loss(model,train_x,train_y))
for _ in range(80):train_step(model,optimizer,train_x,train_y)
# Transfer the device result to the host for an independent NumPy comparison.
# Transfer the device result to the host for an independent NumPy comparison.
scores=np.asarray(model(test_x))
labels=np.asarray(test_y)
predictions=scores.argmax(axis=-1)
# Reduce along axis=-1 to compute `shifted`.
shifted=scores-scores.max(axis=-1,keepdims=True)
# Reduce along axis=-1 to compute `reference_loss`.
reference_loss=np.mean(np.log(np.exp(shifted).sum(axis=-1))-shifted[np.arange(len(labels)),labels])
np.testing.assert_allclose(loss(model,test_x,test_y),reference_loss,rtol=1e-5,atol=1e-6)
confusion=np.zeros((2,2),dtype=int)
np.add.at(confusion,(labels,predictions),1)
accuracy=np.mean(predictions==labels)
assert confusion.sum()==24 and np.isclose(np.trace(confusion)/24,accuracy)
assert accuracy>=.9 and float(loss(model,train_x,train_y))<initial*.3
print('Held-out loss:',reference_loss,'accuracy:',accuracy,'confusion:\n',confusion)
buildSteps.explanation: The output is a measured CPU result for synthetic bars. No MNIST, TPU, or throughput claim is implied.

content.code:
# Step 1 — 1. Generate two disjoint synthetic splits: Two seeds produce separate examples.
from flax import nnx
import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp
import numpy as np
import optax
def bars(seed,n,noise=.08):
    rng=np.random.default_rng(seed)
    images=np.zeros((n,8,8,1),np.float32)
    labels=np.arange(n,dtype=np.int32)%2
    for i,label in enumerate(labels):
        position=int(rng.integers(2,6))
        if label==0:images[i,position,:,0]=1.
        else:images[i,:,position,0]=1.
    # Accumulate the next contribution into `images`.
    images+=rng.normal(0,noise,images.shape).astype(np.float32)
    return jnp.array(images),jnp.array(labels)
train_x,train_y=bars(20,48)
test_x,test_y=bars(21,24)
# Check tensor shape invariant: `train_x.shape==(48,8,8,1) and test_x.shape==(24,8,8,1)`
assert train_x.shape==(48,8,8,1) and test_x.shape==(24,8,8,1)
assert not np.array_equal(np.asarray(train_x[:24]),np.asarray(test_x))

# Step 2 — 2. Build and independently inspect the convolution
# Define `BarCNN` module / container with explicit state and forward pass:
class BarCNN(nnx.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        rngs=nnx.Rngs(0)
        self.conv=nnx.Conv(1,4,(3,3),padding='VALID',rngs=rngs)
        self.head=nnx.Linear(4,2,rngs=rngs)
    def __call__(self,x):
        features=jnp.mean(nnx.relu(self.conv(x)),axis=(1,2))
        return self.head(features)
model=BarCNN()
raw=model.conv(train_x[:1])
# Check tensor shape invariant: `raw.shape==(1,6,6,4)`
assert raw.shape==(1,6,6,4)
# Transfer the device result to the host for an independent NumPy comparison.
patch=np.asarray(train_x[0,:3,:3,:])
# Transfer the device result to the host for an independent NumPy comparison.
kernel=np.asarray(model.conv.kernel[...])
expected=np.sum(patch*kernel[:,:,:,0])+np.asarray(model.conv.bias[...])[0]
np.testing.assert_allclose(raw[0,0,0,0],expected,rtol=1e-5,atol=1e-6)
def loss(m,x,y):return jnp.mean(optax.softmax_cross_entropy_with_integer_labels(m(x),y))
optimizer=nnx.Optimizer(model,optax.adam(.03),wrt=nnx.Param)
@nnx.jit
def train_step(m,o,x,y):
    value,grads=nnx.value_and_grad(loss)(m,x,y)
    # Apply the parameter gradients to the mutable Flax model and optimizer state.
    o.update(m,grads)
    return value

# Step 3 — 3. Fit, then measure the held-out split once: The output is a measured CPU result for synthetic bars.
initial=float(loss(model,train_x,train_y))
for _ in range(80):train_step(model,optimizer,train_x,train_y)
# Transfer the device result to the host for an independent NumPy comparison.
# Transfer the device result to the host for an independent NumPy comparison.
scores=np.asarray(model(test_x))
labels=np.asarray(test_y)
predictions=scores.argmax(axis=-1)
# Subtract each example’s largest class logit before exponentiation for numerical stability.
shifted=scores-scores.max(axis=-1,keepdims=True)
# The log-sum-exp term normalizes over classes; the indexed term selects each true class.
reference_loss=np.mean(np.log(np.exp(shifted).sum(axis=-1))-shifted[np.arange(len(labels)),labels])
np.testing.assert_allclose(loss(model,test_x,test_y),reference_loss,rtol=1e-5,atol=1e-6)
confusion=np.zeros((2,2),dtype=int)
np.add.at(confusion,(labels,predictions),1)
accuracy=np.mean(predictions==labels)
assert confusion.sum()==24 and np.isclose(np.trace(confusion)/24,accuracy)
assert accuracy>=.9 and float(loss(model,train_x,train_y))<initial*.3
print('Held-out loss:',reference_loss,'accuracy:',accuracy,'confusion:\n',confusion)
content.output: Held-out accuracy is at least \(0.9\) for the fixed fixture; confusion counts total \(24\). The runnable script prints the actual measured loss and counts.

experiments.title: Trace a second patch and a second filter
experiments.prediction: If the spatial location changes to \((2,3)\), which input patch produces that output?
experiments.code:
# Experiment — Trace a second patch and a second filter
patch=np.asarray(test_x[0,2:5,3:6,:])
# Transfer the device result to the host for an independent NumPy comparison.
weights=np.asarray(model.conv.kernel[...])[:,:,:,2]
expected=np.sum(patch*weights)+np.asarray(model.conv.bias[...])[2]
np.testing.assert_allclose(model.conv(test_x[:1])[0,2,3,2],expected,rtol=1e-5,atol=1e-6)
experiments.output: The output uses rows \(2\)–\(4\) and columns \(3\)–\(5\) of the input.
experiments.explanation: The same learned filter is reused at each valid location; changing the output coordinate changes the patch, not the filter.

experiments.title: Predict the chance classifier
experiments.prediction: On a balanced held-out split, what is the accuracy of always predicting class zero?
experiments.code:
# Experiment — Predict the chance classifier: A majority or constant-label baseline is part of evaluation.
always_zero=np.zeros_like(labels)
baseline=np.mean(always_zero==labels)
assert baseline==.5
baseline_confusion=np.zeros((2,2),dtype=int)
np.add.at(baseline_confusion,(labels,always_zero),1)
# Transfer the device result to the host for an independent NumPy comparison.
np.testing.assert_array_equal(baseline_confusion,np.array([[12,0],[12,0]]))
experiments.explanation: A majority or constant-label baseline is part of evaluation. A good-looking class-specific count alone can hide a useless predictor.

practice.title: Read a confusion matrix as conditional rates
practice.prompt: Normalize each confusion-matrix row by its true-class count. Explain the diagonal and verify that weighting class recalls by class counts reproduces overall accuracy. Then remove a class in a constructed case and report its recall as undefined.
practice.hint: Keep the integer counts; a normalized row without a count hides how much evidence supports it.
practice.solution:
# Read a confusion matrix as conditional rates (Transfer): Each row asks where examples of one true class went.
# Reduce along axis=1 to compute `counts`.
counts=confusion.sum(axis=1)
rates=np.divide(confusion,counts[:,None],out=np.full(confusion.shape,np.nan),where=counts[:,None]!=0)
np.testing.assert_allclose(rates.sum(axis=1),np.ones(2))
np.testing.assert_allclose((np.diag(rates)*counts).sum()/counts.sum(),accuracy)
missing=np.array([[3,1],[0,0]])
# Reduce along axis=1 to compute `n`.
n=missing.sum(axis=1)
missing_rates=np.divide(missing,n[:,None],out=np.full(missing.shape,np.nan),where=n[:,None]!=0)
# Ensure all array elements remain finite: `np.isnan(missing_rates[1]).all()`
assert np.isnan(missing_rates[1]).all()
print('True-class counts:',counts,'row-normalized confusion:',rates)
print('Absent class recall: undefined, not zero.')
practice.explanation: Each row asks where examples of one true class went. A missing class has no observed recall; assigning zero confuses missing evidence with demonstrated failure.

inputs: Normalize each confusion-matrix row by its true-class count. Explain the diagonal and verify that weighting class recalls by class counts reproduces overall accuracy. Then remove a class in a constructed case and report its recall as undefined.

practice.title: Catch a channel-order mistake
practice.prompt: Transpose NHWC images to NCHW and show why this convolution rejects them. Repair the layout and compare predictions.
practice.hint: The final axis is the input-channel dimension for NNX Conv.
practice.solution:
# Catch a channel-order mistake (Intermediate)
wrong=jnp.transpose(test_x[:2],(0,3,1,2))
caught=False
try:model(wrong)
except (ValueError,TypeError):caught=True
assert caught
# Rearrange tensor axes to match the required layout for `repaired`.
repaired=jnp.transpose(wrong,(0,2,3,1))
np.testing.assert_allclose(model(repaired),model(test_x[:2]),rtol=1e-6)
practice.explanation: The mistaken array has eight channels where the layer expects one. Explicit layout conversion is the repair; changing the declared channel count would silently change the model task.

inputs: Transpose NHWC images to NCHW and show why this convolution rejects them. Repair the layout and compare predictions.
outputs: The failure case and repaired NHWC output/prediction comparison.
invariants: The input batch follows the convolution module’s declared spatial/channel axis order.
hints: The final axis is the input-channel dimension for NNX Conv.

content.question: What does spatial mean pooling discard in this classifier?
options: The exact location of local responses
content.explanation: Pooling summarizes each feature channel over positions. This can support orientation classification, but it cannot preserve exact bar coordinates.
content.diagnosis: Before tuning, inspect sample labels and input layout. Validate a convolution patch numerically, inspect prediction counts, and compare the constant baseline. If all predictions choose one class, examine class balance, score ranges, and per-class errors. If held-out samples equal training samples, repair the split before reporting metrics.
takeaways: Generate images with an explicit label rule
Pool spatial responses and retain class scores
Read a confusion matrix rather than a success label

visual.reading: The top heatmap has pixel columns on the horizontal axis and pixel rows on the vertical axis; its color bar is pixel value. This held-out example shows a bright horizontal band around row 3. In the lower heatmap, row labels are actual orientation and columns are predicted orientation; the color bar counts examples. Its observed cells are ([[12,0],[0,12]]), with all 24 images on the diagonal.

The zero errors apply only to this synthetic split.

Its dark horizontal stripe is near row \(3\); the faint variation elsewhere is added noise. This color bar measures pixel value, so the picture is an input to the classifier. The lower panel summarizes all held-out predictions. Rows are actual classes and columns are predicted classes. The two diagonal cells contain \(12\) each; both off-diagonal cells contain zero. diagram.title: Pixels behind one convolution output
diagram.prediction: What stays shared when the kernel moves?
diagram.reading: The highlighted purple square is one \(3\times3\) receptive field on a \(5\times5\) input. Its nine selected cells contribute, with their corresponding filter weights, to one output location. Move the square one cell at a time: at stride one and no padding it has three valid positions across and three down, producing a \(3\times3\) map. The filter is reused at each position. Then compare this shape example with the trained \(8\times8\) inputs, which produce \(6\times6\) spatial outputs; the diagram shows the indexing rule, not learned filter values.
diagram.alt: The purple square selects one three-by-three patch within a five-by-five input. Each selected cell contributes to one output under the declared convolution. Moving the patch reuses weights. This separate shape example has three valid positions per axis at stride one without padding; it does not display learned weights.

optionFeedback: Pooling summarizes each feature channel over positions. This can support orientation classification, but it cannot preserve exact bar coordinates.
A mean over spatial axes preserves the channel axis. Inspect which axes disappear from the output shape.
Convolutional channels can encode orientation responses before pooling. The direct information lost here is the exact spatial arrangement.
